opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic reason is just a matter of scale. If you look at how the economy actually allocates its resources, R&D is a pretty small fraction of total output. In the US, total R&D spending is something like two to three percent of GDP, and if you narrow that down to the kind of frontier research people usually have in mind when they talk about AI automating R&D, it's even smaller. Meanwhile, labor compensation is something like half or more of GDP. So if you ask where the immediate economic value of a system that can substitute for human cognitive labor lies, the overwhelming majority of it is in doing the ordinary work that people across the economy do every day, not in the narrow slice of activity that is research.

Now, the standard counterargument is that R&D is special because it has these compounding effects. If you automate research, you get better technology, which makes everything else more productive, and maybe you get a fast feedback loop where AI improves AI. I don't think that's crazy, but I think it's overstated, for a couple of reasons.

One is that research output doesn't seem to be bottlenecked purely on cognitive labor. A lot of progress, including in AI itself, has come from scaling up compute, from experiments, from building physical infrastructure, from learning by doing as you deploy technology widely. If you look at historical estimates, a substantial part of productivity growth doesn't come from formal R&D at all. It comes from diffusion, from firms adopting existing technologies, from accumulated experience in production. So if you only put AI into labs, you're cutting yourself off from many of the channels through which progress actually happens.

The second reason is complementarity. Research labor and other inputs are complements. If you have an enormous number of AI researchers but the same amount of compute, the same amount of lab equipment, the same capital stock, you run into diminishing returns pretty quickly. Whereas if you deploy AI broadly, you grow the whole economy, which means more investment, more compute, more capital to go along with all that research capacity. Broad deployment is in a sense what funds and enables the research.

And third, practically speaking, the revenue matters. The companies building these systems need enormous amounts of capital to keep scaling, and that capital ultimately comes from the value the systems create when they're actually used. If you deploy narrowly for R&D, you're leaving most of that value on the table, which means you scale more slowly, not faster.

So my view is that the picture where a small number of AI systems quietly automate research in a lab and then everything explodes from there is less likely than a picture where AI gets deployed across the economy, does a growing share of all kinds of work, and growth accelerates because of that broad automation. The broad deployment is where most of the value is, and I think it's also where most of the acceleration ultimately comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says broad AI deployment grows the economy, creating more investment and capital that fund and enable research.

r002.rationale: It describes research inputs as complementary and says fixed compute, equipment, and capital create diminishing returns, but does not state that long-run growth requires all factors of production to scale.

r003.rationale: It compares R&D spending with labor compensation and mentions productivity from diffusion and adoption, but does not attribute more growth to scaling labor and capital than to R&D.

r004.rationale: It predicts broad automation will drive more value and acceleration than narrow R&D, but does not specifically predict that scaling labor and capital will remain the larger source of growth.

fable-5.1.text:
So the basic reason is just that the labor market is enormous and R&D is a very small slice of it. If you look at the global economy, total compensation to labor is on the order of fifty, sixty trillion dollars a year. Spending on research and development, even if you're generous about what counts, is maybe two or three trillion. So just in terms of where the value sits, the overwhelming majority of it is in ordinary work, people doing jobs that aren't research.

Now, the counterargument people make is that R&D is special because it has this compounding effect. You automate the research, the research produces better technology, that feeds back, and so on. And I don't dismiss that. But I think people overestimate how much R&D, narrowly construed, is actually the bottleneck on economic growth. If you look at how productivity improvements have actually happened historically, a huge fraction of it is not someone in a lab discovering a new principle. It's diffusion, it's learning by doing, it's a million small adjustments made by people on the ground who are actually deploying the technology and running into problems. Those improvements happen in the economy, not in the research department.

So if you have an AI system that can only do R&D, you've captured a narrow sliver of what makes the economy grow. You get better ideas, but you still have to get those ideas implemented by humans, who are slow and expensive and limited in number. Whereas if you have a system that can do broad labor, then you've not only captured that fifty trillion dollars directly, you've also captured the implementation side, the experimentation side, all of the tacit knowledge that gets generated by actually doing things in the world. And that feeds back into R&D too, because a lot of the inputs to good research come from contact with real problems.

There's also a more practical point, which is that broad deployment is what generates the revenue that pays for the compute. If you're going to be scaling these systems up by orders of magnitude, somebody has to fund that, and the way it gets funded is by the systems doing economically valuable work at scale. Deploying narrowly to a few thousand researchers doesn't get you there. So even from the perspective of someone who only cares about accelerating R&D, I think the path runs through broad deployment anyway.

r001.rationale: It presents broad labor deployment as advancing R&D through implementation, experimentation, tacit knowledge, and contact with real-world problems.

r002.rationale: It does not state that long-run growth requires all factors of production to scale.

r003.rationale: It compares labor compensation with R&D spending, but does not attribute more growth to scaling labor and capital than to R&D.

r004.rationale: It favors broad deployment and discusses historical productivity improvements, but does not predict that scaling labor and capital will remain a larger source of growth than R&D even with AI.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by distinguishing the size of the opportunity from how much leverage a particular application might have. R&D can be very high leverage: a discovery can improve productivity across the economy. But most economic activity isn’t R&D. It’s producing goods, delivering services, managing organizations, and doing all the other work that people get paid to do. If AI can perform a substantial fraction of those tasks, there’s an enormous amount of value available directly.

With R&D, there are also several steps between doing the intellectual work and realizing the economic benefit. You might develop a better technology, but then you need to test it, build facilities, get organizations to adopt it, and so on. Making research faster doesn’t necessarily make all of those other steps faster.

So I wouldn’t say broad labor deployment must always be more valuable. If AI research led to much more capable AI, for example, that could have an extraordinary payoff. But you don’t need to assume that kind of breakthrough to get a very large economic impact from automating ordinary work. That’s the reason I’d put so much weight on the broader labor market.

r001.rationale: The response describes broad labor deployment as a direct source of economic value; it does not identify it as an indirect way to advance R&D.

r002.rationale: It does not state that long-run growth requires all factors of production to scale.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about growth accounting or compare growth attributed to labor and capital versus R&D.

r004.rationale: It does not predict that scaling labor and capital will remain a larger source of growth than R&D with AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is the size of the market. R&D is very important for economic growth, but it’s a relatively small fraction of what we currently spend our resources on. Most people are doing things other than research. So if you have AI that can substitute for labor across a broad range of tasks, there’s an enormous amount of economic value you can capture, even without making any new scientific discoveries.

With R&D, there are also several steps between having a better idea and getting an economic payoff. You might discover a better material, but then you need to test it, build manufacturing capacity, and get people to adopt it. Making the research part cheaper doesn’t necessarily make all those other steps cheaper or faster.

That doesn’t mean the long-run value of automating research couldn’t be much larger. If AI substantially accelerates technological progress, that could eventually dominate. But that’s a different claim from saying that deploying AI in R&D is the biggest immediate economic opportunity. Broad labor automation has a much more direct route to producing value: you’re doing things that people already pay a very large amount of money to have done.

r001.rationale: The response presents broad labor automation as a direct source of economic value, but does not identify it as an indirect way to advance R&D.

r002.rationale: It does not state that long-run growth requires all factors of production to scale.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about growth accounting or compares growth from labor and capital scaling with growth from R&D.

r004.rationale: It does not predict that scaling labor and capital will remain a larger source of growth than R&D even with AI.
